newsitem.title: FRANCE: EP's Gil-Robles plays down double voting row.
newsitem.headline: EP's Gil-Robles plays down double voting row.

text.p: The European Parliament's new president, at the centre of controversy about the way he was elected, sought on Wednesday to play down a row over a French deputy who voted for an absent colleague on a divisive report.

Spanish Conservative Jose Maria Gil-Robles told a news conference he hoped to "find a middle way" between calls from the parliament's Socialist group to expel Jean-Claude Pasty and the straightjacket of the assembly's rules.

Gil-Robles told the assembly that Pasty, the leader of the right-wing Union for Europe group, had admitted voting twice on a report on the protection of children during last month's plenary session in Strasbourg
But under the assembly's rules sanctions had to be imposed within 48 hours, and the decision to refer the offence to a meeting of the parliament's political leaders meant this deadline had expired.
His explanations caused uproar in the parliament on Wednesday.
"I am totally dissatisfied with the reacton of Mr Gil-Robles, who seems to be distancing himself from the will of the House," Socialist leader Pauline Green said in a written statement.
Green said she would challenge the president during a meeting of political group leaders later in the day.
Gil-Robles told reporters he would ask the committee examining parliament's internal rules to look at the possibility of changing the system.
The December vote on the report on children split members of the parliament over whether the definition of a family should include homes run by single parents, and unmarried and homosexual couples.

British Socialist John Tomlinson complained that in a vote on a particularly sensitive amendment Pasty appeared to have voted for his absent neighbour as well as for himself -- a practice known as "playing the piano".
Pasty said it had been a mistake. "I plead guilty to an error of manipulation," he said.
"Perhaps we have to change the format of the hemicycle (Parliament's chamber) if it is so easy to simultaneously get your hands in two voting machines," Tomlinson commented.

Gil-Robles, who will lead the assembly to its next elections in June 1999, repeated on Wednesday his rebuttal of protests from parliament's smaller groups that he was undemocratically bulldozed in by the assembly's two political powerhouses, the Socialists and Conservatives.
He pointed out that the speaker of the British House of Commons was also elected through a pact between the two largest parties.
